newsitem.title: VIETNAM: IMF official urges Vietnam to kickstart reforms.
newsitem.headline: IMF official urges Vietnam to kickstart reforms.

text.p: An International Monetary Fund official has urged Vietnam to launch a new generation of outward-looking economic reforms with a warning that unless it does so the economy will suffer.

Michael Bell, the IMF's Hanoi representative, said in a statement published by Vietnam's official press on Thursday that recent problems in the economy indicated a need for an early re-start of the Doi Moi (Renovation) process first launched in the late 1980s.

"What is needed at present is a new generation of reforms, both more rapid and more comprehensive," he said. "Sustaining growth in the next few years may depend much more on strong reform than in the past."
Bell said that although flows of external resources into Vietnam were likely to continue, it could not count on major new sources of external finance to bolster economic progress.
"Therefore, the stimulus for growth in the late 1990s will need to come from comprehensive reform to boost domestic saving and to maintain the confidence of foreign investors," he said.

He added that Hanoi's key goal should be to make the economy open and outward-oriented and said areas where reforms were most needed included trade liberalisation, the banking sector, and enterprise reform plus the need to reduce bureaucratic bottle-necks.
"Of great importance is an improvement in the quantity and quality of economic data available to the general public, enabling economic agents to make rational decisions," he said.
Bell's comments follow a lengthy period of political inertia which has had an impact on confidence among investors in the communist country's ability to manage a market economy.

A frank article in the Communist Party's Nhan Dan newspaper this week pointed out that there were more attractive investment environments in East Asia and said the number of foreign direct investment projects licensed in the first six months of this year had fallen by 23 and 35 percent respectively from 1996 and 1995.
Bell said that based on available information recent problems in the financial and other sectors could be overcome.

"With the overall macroeconomic situation still in good shape, the country has a golden opportunity to concentrate on longer term issues and to develop the next generation of reforms," he said. "Without those reforms, the economy will slow down sooner or later."
